# On Having a Thousand Words and Nothing in Particular to Say

There's a peculiar kind of freedom in being told you have exactly one thousand words and no subject. Most writing begins with a constraint that isn't quantity but topic—write about your summer vacation, write about climate policy, write a eulogy, write an apology. The number of words is supposed to take care of itself, shrinking or swelling to fit the size of the thought. But here the thought has to grow to fit the number, like water poured into a strange-shaped glass, and that reversal changes everything about how the sentences want to behave.

I think most people, if handed this assignment, would panic slightly and then default to a list. Ten things I believe. Five places I've been. A ranking of something. Lists are the natural shelter for a mind without a destination, because a list lets you pretend you're being efficient even while you're stalling. I want to resist that, not out of some principled stance against lists, which are a perfectly good form, but because it would be too easy, and ease is rarely interesting to read.

So instead: what is a word, exactly, before it's used? Sitting alone, unconnected, a word is almost nothing—a little bundle of sound and convention waiting for context to make it mean something. "Bank" means nothing in particular until it's leaning against a river or holding your savings. "Right" is directionless until it's politically inflected or morally certain or simply the opposite of left. Words are strange in that they have the appearance of solidity—you can look one up, find its definition, point to it on a page—while actually being almost entirely dependent on their neighbors for meaning. A word alone is a key without a lock. It's only in combination that anything happens.

This is maybe why writing with no topic feels both harder and easier than writing with one. Harder because there's no lock to aim the key at; easier because any key will do, since there's no specific door I'm trying to open. I could write about the weather, which is famously what people resort to when they have nothing to say to each other, proof that even silence needs scaffolding. I could write about the room I'm in, the slight hum of whatever electronic thing is always humming in rooms now, the specific quality of afternoon light that makes everything look like it's already a memory of itself.

I keep noticing that I'm writing about writing, which is a kind of cheat, like a painter who can't think what to paint so paints a picture of an empty canvas. But maybe that's not a cheat so much as an honest report. If you ask someone what's on their mind and their mind is genuinely blank, the most truthful answer is a description of the blankness itself—the shape of it, the texture, whether it feels peaceful or anxious, whether it's the blankness of contentment or the blankness of dread. Blankness is not nothing. It has weather.

There's a thing that happens around word four hundred of an assignment like this, a kind of false floor. You think you're about halfway and you check and you're not, you're barely a third through, and there's a small interior groan, the same groan you might make on a long drive when you check the map and the distance hasn't shrunk nearly as much as the time you've spent driving would suggest. Time and word count have an uneasy relationship. Ten minutes of fluent writing might produce two hundred words or it might produce twenty, depending on whether the sentences are arriving or being extracted, like teeth, one at a time, with pliers.

I wonder sometimes whether length itself carries a kind of emotional charge independent of content. A short text message feels curt even if it's friendly; a long email feels earnest even if it's boring. We've trained ourselves, maybe without meaning to, to read quantity as a signal of investment, so that "fine." and "Fine, I think it's totally fine, really, no worries at all, just let me know" register completely differently even though they might describe the exact same state of mind. The thousand words I'm filling now are themselves a kind of message before they're anything else—a demonstration that something can be produced on demand, at length, without buckling. Maybe that's all this is: proof of stamina, dressed up as reflection.

But stamina for what, exactly? Nobody needs a thousand words about nothing. And yet there's something almost moving about the willingness to generate them anyway—the way a person might hum a tune with no audience, not because the tune matters but because humming is itself a small assertion that you're alive and your throat works and the air is moving through you in a shape that pleases you, however briefly. Writing without a destination might be the verbal equivalent of pacing. You're not trying to get anywhere. You're just moving because moving is something a body, or a mind, does when it's not pinned down by purpose.

I notice the count creeping toward its limit now, the way you notice the gas gauge dropping on a long stretch of highway with no exits, a low hum of awareness that doesn't change your behavior but sits alongside it. There isn't a tidy conclusion coming. I don't think this kind of writing earns one—a piece that begins with no subject doesn't owe you a moral, a turn, a resolution, any more than the weather owes you a reason for the clouds. It can simply stop, the way conversations sometimes stop, not because everything has been said but because the talking has, for now, run its course, and what's left is just the quiet that was always underneath it, patiently waiting its turn.
